title: Plate tectonics
examples: What is the difference between a divergent and a convergent boundary?
How does convection help move the tectonic plates?
Can you show me an example of evidence for plate movement?

explain.say: Today we are learning about plate tectonics. This explains how the Earth's surface moves. The Earth's outer shell is broken into large pieces. These pieces are called tectonic plates.
Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: two plates meeting. Look at the ocean plate, the continental plate and the trench. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.
The boundaries between these plates are very important. There are three main types of boundaries. These are divergent, convergent, and transform boundaries.
At divergent boundaries, plates pull away from each other. Magma rises up to fill the gap. This process creates new crustal material. Think of it like pulling apart a giant puzzle.

draw.text: Divergent: Plates pull apart; new crust forms

explain.say: At convergent boundaries, plates push towards each other. One plate often slides under another. This process is called subduction. This can cause deep ocean trenches.
Transform boundaries involve plates sliding past each other horizontally. Crust grinds along the edges. This movement causes a lot of shaking, which we call earthquakes.

draw.text: Transform: Plates slide past each other; earthquakes

explain.say: The movement of the plates is driven by convection currents. Heat deep inside the Earth causes the mantle rock to move slowly. Hot material rises, and cool material sinks.

faq.q: What is the difference between magma and lava?
faq.a: Magma is molten rock found beneath the Earth's surface. Lava is molten rock that has reached the Earth's surface. You might hear them used interchangeably, but they are different.
asks: What is lava when it comes out?

faq.q: Do all plate boundaries cause earthquakes?
faq.a: No, while most boundaries are associated with earthquakes, the type and size vary greatly. Some movement might cause tremors but not major quakes.
asks: Are earthquakes only at plate edges?
What causes the shaking at plate boundaries?

faq.a: Subduction is the process where one tectonic plate slides beneath another plate. The denser plate sinks into the Earth's mantle. This happens at convergent boundaries.
asks: Does one plate go under another?
What happens when plates crash together?

faq.q: How fast do the plates move?
faq.a: The plates move very slowly, at rates similar to the speed your fingernails grow. This movement takes millions of years to cause major changes.
asks: Is plate movement fast or slow?
How quickly does the Earth's crust move?

faq.q: What is evidence for plate movement?
faq.a: Scientists look at things like matching fossils on continents and patterns of ancient rock types. These suggest the continents were once joined together.
asks: How do we know the continents moved?

facts: The Earth's lithosphere is broken into many large plates.
Divergent boundaries create new crust as plates pull apart.
Subduction occurs at convergent boundaries when one plate sinks.
Convection currents in the mantle drive the movement of the plates.

quiz.say: When two plates slide past each other, the boundary type is:
quiz.why: Sliding past each other horizontally defines a transform boundary.

wrong.1: This is when plates pull apart, not slide sideways.
wrong.2: This describes plates crashing together, not sliding past.
wrong.3: Subduction is a process that happens at a boundary, not the boundary type itself.

quiz.say: What process causes the movement of the tectonic plates?
quiz.why: Heat transfer through the mantle via convection currents powers the plate movement.

wrong.0: Tidal forces are caused by gravity and affect oceans, not the deep mantle.
wrong.1: Magma pressure is involved, but convection currents are the larger driving mechanism.
wrong.3: While rotation is a force, it is not the primary driver of plate movement.

quiz.say: Fossil evidence showing matching ancient life across continents suggests:
quiz.why: Matching fossils suggest the landmasses were once joined together in a supercontinent.

wrong.1: Fossils are evidence of the landmasses' past positions, not transported by water.
wrong.2: Volcanoes create rock, but fossils show life that existed in place.
wrong.3: Wind erosion affects the surface, but fossils record life over long periods.
